questions.title: Which of the following induces secondary signals augmenting BCR-complex antigen recognition, important for B-cell activation?
questions.question: Which of the following induces secondary signals augmenting antigen recognition signals of the BCR complex and is important for B cell activation?

options.A: Complement component (C3d) acting on complement receptor 2 on B lymphocytes
options.B: CTLA-4 on activated T helper cells
options.C: PAMPs on microbes acting on Toll like receptors on B-lymphocytes

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. C3d engaging complement receptor 2 (CR2/CD21) genuinely is one of the two costimulatory second signals — but option c (PAMP-TLR engagement) is also genuine, so 'a alone' is incomplete.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CTLA-4 is an inhibitory checkpoint receptor expressed on activated T cells that dampens T-cell costimulation; it plays no role in delivering a B-cell second signal.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. PAMP recognition by Toll-like receptors on B cells genuinely is one of the two costimulatory second signals — but option a (C3d-CR2) is also genuine, so 'c alone' is incomplete.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Because CTLA-4 (b) is not a genuine B-cell costimulatory signal — it is a T-cell inhibitory checkpoint molecule — 'both a and b' cannot be correct.
explanations.E: Correct. Naive B-cell activation is augmented by two distinct, genuine second-signal pathways alongside BCR-antigen engagement: C3d (deposited on antigen during complement activation) engaging complement receptor 2 on the B cell, and pathogen-associated molecular patterns on microbes engaging Toll-like receptors on the B cell. CTLA-4 is unrelated to either pathway, since it is a T-cell inhibitory receptor, not a B-cell signalling molecule, which is exactly why 'both a and c' — not 'both a and b' — is the correct pairing.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C3d-CR2 and PAMP-TLR engagement, not CTLA-4, as the two genuine B-cell costimulatory second signals.

questions.title: The phenomenon of affinity maturation occurring in prolonged and repeated infections is due to:
questions.question: The phenomenon of affinity maturation of antibodies occurring in prolonged and repeated infections is due to:

options.A: High mutation rate of proliferating B cells at late phase of humoral immune response
options.B: PAMPs on microbes acting on Toll like receptors on B-lymphocytes
options.C: Complement component (C3d) acting on complement receptor 2 on B lymphocytes
options.D: Costimulation of B lymphocytes by CD28 on macrophages

explanations.A: Correct. In prolonged or repeated infections, germinal-centre B cells proliferating at the late phase of the humoral response acquire somatic point mutations in their immunoglobulin genes at an unusually high rate, and B cells whose mutated receptor binds antigen more tightly are selectively expanded. This progressive selection for higher-affinity clones is exactly what affinity maturation means, and it explains why late, repeated or prolonged exposure yields tighter-binding antibody than an early response does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PAMP-TLR engagement delivers an activation/costimulatory signal to the B cell; it does not drive the somatic mutation process that raises antibody affinity over time.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C3d-CR2 engagement is likewise a costimulatory activation signal, not the mechanism generating the mutations responsible for affinity maturation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CD28-mediated costimulation of B lymphocytes by macrophages is not how affinity maturation is generated; affinity maturation is driven by somatic hypermutation within proliferating germinal-centre B cells, not by this costimulatory pathway.

questions.learning_objective: State that affinity maturation in prolonged/repeated infection results from a high somatic mutation rate among late-phase proliferating B cells.

questions.title: Affinity maturation of antibodies at the late phase of the humoral immune response is due to mutations in:
questions.question: Affinity maturation of antibodies at the late phase of humoral immune response is due to mutations in:

explanations.A: Correct. Affinity maturation results from somatic hypermutation targeted to the immunoglobulin variable (V) region — the segment encoding the antigen-binding domain of both heavy and light chains. Because the mutations concentrate in the V region rather than in a constant-region exon, they can improve antigen-binding affinity for the specific epitope without altering the antibody's isotype or effector function, which is exactly the pattern affinity maturation describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CH1 is a heavy-chain constant-region exon (part of the Fab arm's constant domain), not the site of affinity-raising mutations.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CH2 is a heavy-chain constant-region exon involved in effector function (e.g. complement fixation for some isotypes), not the site of affinity-maturing mutations.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CH3 is a heavy-chain constant-region exon, contributing to isotype identity and effector function, not to antigen-binding affinity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. CL is the light-chain constant-region exon; affinity-maturation mutations concentrate in the variable, not the constant, light-chain region.

questions.learning_objective: Localise affinity-maturation mutations to the immunoglobulin V region, distinguishing it from the constant-region exons.

questions.title: Which of the following statements describes monoclonal antibodies?
questions.question: Which of the following statements describes Monoclonal antibodies?

options.A: Antibodies sharing epitopes from different species
options.B: Antibodies against a single epitope and produced from a single clone of immortal cells
options.C: Antibodies with different affinities for the same antigen that induced them
options.D: Produced by fusion of a normal plasma cell with a B cell producing antibodies against a single epitope
options.E: Induced in the lab by B lymphocyte activation by endotoxin

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sharing epitopes across species describes cross-reactivity, not the defining property of a monoclonal antibody, which is single-clone, single-epitope specificity.
explanations.B: Correct. A monoclonal antibody is, by definition, produced by a single clone of immortalised antibody-secreting cells and is therefore directed against one single epitope with one uniform affinity — unlike a polyclonal response, which contains antibodies of differing affinities against multiple epitopes on a single immunising antigen. This distinction between a mixed polyclonal pool and a single, uniform monoclonal product is exactly what the question's five options are testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Antibodies with differing affinities for the same antigen describe a polyclonal response, the opposite of the uniform, single-clone monoclonal pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The real hybridoma technique fuses a normal antibody-secreting plasma (or B) cell with an immortal myeloma (tumour) cell, not with another B cell producing antibody against a single epitope; this option misstates the fusion partner.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endotoxin-driven B-lymphocyte activation in vitro is not how monoclonal antibodies are manufactured; the standard method is hybridoma fusion with an immortal myeloma cell line.

questions.learning_objective: Define a monoclonal antibody as one produced from a single immortalised clone and directed against a single epitope.

questions.title: The process by which IgG and/or C3b enhance phagocytosis is called:
questions.question: The process by which IgG and/or C3b enhance phagocytosis is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Opsonization is the process in which IgG antibody and/or the complement fragment C3b coat (tag) a microbial antigen, so that phagocytes bearing Fc receptors (for IgG) or complement receptors (for C3b) recognise and engulf the coated particle far more efficiently. This antibody-and-complement-mediated tagging is exactly what 'enhancing phagocytosis' names, distinguishing it from mechanisms that act on the microbe's ability to bind host cells (neutralization) or that kill an antibody-coated host cell (ADCC).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neutralization is antibody blocking a microbe or toxin from binding host cells directly; it does not describe IgG/C3b-mediated enhancement of phagocytic uptake.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity) is the antibody-directed killing of an already antibody-coated target cell by an effector cell such as an NK cell, not the tagging of free antigen for phagocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Agglutination is antibody cross-linking particulate antigen into clumps; it does not describe enhanced phagocytic engulfment of a single tagged particle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 'Sensitization' as a distractor here refers loosely to antibody coating a target for a later effector step (as in ADCC or complement fixation), not specifically to the IgG/C3b-mediated phagocytosis-enhancement process named opsonization.

questions.learning_objective: Identify opsonization as the process by which IgG and/or C3b enhance phagocytosis.

questions.title: Antibody binding to microbial epitopes or soluble molecules that blocks host-cell binding is termed:
questions.question: The binding of antibodies to microbial epitopes or soluble molecules in a manner that inhibits the ability of these microbes to bind to host cell surfaces is termed

explanations.A: Incorrect. Agglutination is antibody cross-linking particulate antigens into visible clumps; it is a separate effector mechanism from blocking host-cell binding.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complement activation is a distinct antibody-triggered pathway (via C1q engagement) with its own downstream products (opsonization, anaphylatoxins, MAC), not the direct blocking of microbe-host binding described here.
explanations.C: Correct. Neutralization is the antibody effector mechanism in which antibody binds directly to epitopes on a microbe or to a soluble molecule such as a toxin, physically blocking that microbe or toxin from attaching to and entering a host cell — a mechanism that can act without complement or phagocytes at all. Because it acts directly on the antibody-microbe or antibody-toxin interaction, neutralization can protect a host cell even without any complement or phagocyte participation at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Opsonization enhances phagocytic uptake of an already-tagged particle; it does not itself describe blocking the microbe's binding to host cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Precipitation is antibody cross-linking soluble antigen into an insoluble lattice, a different phenomenon from blocking a microbe's host-cell attachment.

questions.learning_objective: Identify neutralization as antibody binding that blocks a microbe or toxin from binding host cell surfaces.

questions.title: An important feature of thymus-independent antigens is:
questions.question: An important feature of Thymic independent antigens is:

options.A: They are composed of a hapten conjugated to a carrier protein
options.B: They have repeated epitopes that cross link membrane bound immunoglobulins on B cells
options.C: They elicit a memory response on re-exposure to them
options.D: They lead to secretion of all isotypes of antibodies
options.E: Ubiquitous antigens in the body displayed on MHC molecules for T cells during their development

explanations.A: Incorrect. A hapten-carrier conjugate is the classic thymus-DEPENDENT antigen structure, requiring carrier-protein processing and T-cell help — the opposite of a thymus-independent antigen.
explanations.B: Correct. Thymus-independent (TI) antigens, typically bacterial polysaccharides, characteristically carry many repeated copies of the same epitope; this repetitive structure lets a single TI antigen cross-link enough membrane-bound immunoglobulin (BCR) molecules on one B cell to deliver a strong enough signal to activate it without T-cell help. This is why a repetitive polysaccharide, but not a single-copy protein epitope, can activate a B cell without any T-cell help at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. TI antigens do not generate memory B cells; eliciting a memory response on re-exposure is a thymus-dependent, T-cell-help-dependent feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. TI responses are largely restricted to IgM, not secretion of all isotypes; isotype switching to multiple classes requires T-cell help (CD40L-CD40), a thymus-dependent feature.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This describes self antigens displayed on MHC during T-cell thymic education, an unrelated concept to the structural cross-linking feature of thymus-independent antigens.

questions.learning_objective: Identify repeated, cross-linking epitopes as the defining structural feature of thymus-independent antigens.

questions.title: Which of the following is considered a thymus-independent antigen?
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a Thymic independent antigen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Foreign RBCs are cellular antigens whose response involves T-cell-dependent mechanisms (as in allo-immunisation), not the classic TI polysaccharide pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hapten-carrier conjugate is the classic thymus-dependent antigen structure, not thymus-independent.
explanations.C: Correct. Bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), like other repetitive bacterial polysaccharides, is a classic thymus-independent antigen: it activates B cells directly via repeated epitopes and TLR/PAMP recognition, without requiring cognate T-cell help. Its repetitive polysaccharide backbone is exactly the structural feature that lets it cross-link BCR molecules and bypass the need for T-cell help.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bacterial flagellin is a protein antigen; protein antigens require T-cell help and are thymus-dependent, not thymus-independent.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The M protein of Strept pyogenes is likewise a protein antigen and is thymus-dependent, requiring T-cell help for an antibody response.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bacterial lipopolysaccharide as a thymus-independent antigen.

questions.title: Which of the following is a thymus-dependent antigen?
questions.question: Which of the following is a Thymic dependent antigen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pneumococcal capsule is a polysaccharide antigen, the classic thymus-independent pattern, not thymus-dependent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacterial LPS is likewise a polysaccharide-type surface antigen and is thymus-independent.
explanations.C: Correct. The M protein of Streptococcus pyogenes is a protein antigen, and protein antigens are processed and presented on MHC to T cells, making them thymus-dependent — they require cognate T-helper-cell engagement (CD40L-CD40) to generate a full antibody response with isotype switching and memory. Being a protein rather than a polysaccharide is precisely what routes this antigen through MHC-restricted presentation and cognate T-helper engagement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Penicillin is a hapten — a small molecule that is not itself a complete antigen and cannot elicit an antibody response on its own without conjugation to a carrier protein.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a protein antigen (M protein of Strept pyogenes) as thymus-dependent.

questions.title: Activation of a naive B cell requires BCR engagement plus a second signal from:
questions.question: Activation of a naive B cell requires both the engagement of its BCR (membrane bound immunoglobulin) with its specific epitope plus additional secondary signals from

explanations.A: Correct. A naive B cell's activation requires BCR-epitope engagement plus a second signal delivered by CD4+ T-helper-2 (Th2) cells, chiefly via CD40 ligand engaging CD40 on the B cell together with Th2 cytokines (such as IL-4) that support B-cell proliferation, isotype switching and differentiation. Without this CD4+ Th2-derived second signal, BCR-epitope engagement alone is not enough to fully activate a naive, thymus-dependent-antigen-specific B cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CD4+ Th1 cells chiefly support cell-mediated immunity (macrophage activation) via IFN-gamma, not the classic B-cell-help second signal, which is a Th2 (or follicular helper) function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill infected or abnormal host cells directly; they do not deliver the B-cell activation second signal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gamma-delta T cells are an innate-like T-cell population and are not the classic source of B-cell help for a thymus-dependent humoral response.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Dendritic cells present antigen to T cells to initiate their activation, but they are not themselves the source of the CD40L-mediated second signal a naive B cell needs.

questions.learning_objective: Identify CD4+ Th2 cells as the source of the second signal required for naive B-cell activation.

questions.title: Which of the following is characteristic of thymus-independent antigens?
questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of Thymic independent antigens?

options.C: Need activation signals from TH1 cells
options.D: Need activation signals from TH2 cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thymus-independent antigens are multivalent, not univalent; a univalent antigen could not cross-link multiple BCR molecules to deliver a strong enough signal alone.
explanations.B: Correct. Thymus-independent (TI) antigens are characteristically multivalent, carrying many repetitive copies of the same epitope on one molecule, which is precisely what allows them to cross-link enough BCR molecules to activate a B cell without T-cell help. It is exactly this repetitive, cross-linking structure that removes the normal requirement for T-cell help in activating the B cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Needing Th1-cell activation signals is not a feature of thymus-independent antigens; by definition, TI antigens do not need T-cell help at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Likewise, needing Th2-cell activation signals defines the thymus-DEPENDENT pathway, the opposite of thymus-independent activation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Inducing memory B cells is a thymus-dependent feature; thymus-independent responses generate plasma cells without durable memory.

questions.learning_objective: State that thymus-independent antigens are multivalent with repetitive epitopes.

questions.title: A change from an IgM to a predominant IgE response over the course of an allergic reaction is caused by:
questions.question: In a patient who later developed an allergy to a certain antigen, the initial response to the antigen consisted of immunoglobulin of the IgM class. However, overtime, antigen specific IgE came to be predominant. This change from an IgM to an IgE response is caused by

explanations.A: Incorrect. Affinity maturation raises binding affinity for the same isotype and epitope over time; it does not describe a change of isotype from IgM to IgE.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Allelic exclusion restricts a single B cell to expressing only one productively rearranged heavy- and light-chain allele; it has nothing to do with a subsequent change in isotype.
explanations.C: Correct. When the initial IgM response to an antigen is followed, over time, by a predominant antigen-specific IgE response, the change in isotype without a change in antigen specificity is isotype (class) switching, mediated by CD40L-CD40 T-cell help driving class-switch recombination in the antigen-specific B-cell clone. The antigen specificity encoded in the variable region is preserved across the switch, so only the effector-function-determining constant region changes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Junctional diversity is a V(D)J recombination mechanism that generates receptor diversity during B- and T-cell development; it is not the mechanism of a later isotype change.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Somatic hypermutation drives affinity maturation (raising binding affinity within an isotype), not the change of isotype itself, which is isotype switching.

questions.learning_objective: Identify a change from IgM to a predominant IgE response as isotype switching.

questions.title: Point mutations in a re-stimulated memory B cell's variable-region DNA may result in:
questions.question: When a memory B cell is re-stimulated by its specific antigen, small point mutations that accumulate in DNA encoding variable regions of both light and heavy chains may result in

options.B: Isotype switching from IgM to IgG
options.C: DNA chromosomal rearrangement and altered antigen specificity
options.D: Inactivation of either the paternal or maternal variable heavy and light alleles
options.E: Generation of antibody with increased binding affinity for its epitope

explanations.A: Incorrect. Somatic hypermutation refines binding affinity for the SAME epitope; it does not typically generate an entirely new antigen specificity for a different epitope.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A change in isotype (IgM to IgG) is isotype switching, a separate CD40L-driven recombination event, not the result of variable-region point mutations.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA chromosomal rearrangement (V(D)J recombination) occurs during B-cell development to generate the initial receptor, not from small point mutations accumulating after re-stimulation of a memory cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Allelic exclusion (silencing of the non-productively-rearranged allele) is established during early B-cell development, not caused by point mutations accumulating during a later re-stimulation.
explanations.E: Correct. When a memory B cell is re-stimulated by its specific antigen, small point mutations accumulate in the DNA encoding the variable regions of both its light and heavy chains (somatic hypermutation); B cells whose mutated receptor binds antigen with higher affinity are selectively expanded, so the net result is generation of antibody with increased binding affinity for its epitope — this whole process, and its outcome, is what the term affinity maturation names. It does not create an entirely new antigen specificity, switch isotype, cause DNA chromosomal rearrangement, or inactivate a parental allele, all of which are separate mechanisms unrelated to this somatic-hypermutation process.

questions.learning_objective: State that somatic point mutations in re-stimulated memory B cells' variable-region DNA generate antibody of increased binding affinity.

questions.title: Accumulation of point mutations affecting variable-region binding affinity is termed:
questions.question: Accumulation of point mutations that affect light and heavy chain variable regions causing an increase in antibody binding to its specific antigen is termed

explanations.A: Incorrect. Costimulation refers to the second signal (such as CD28-B7 or CD40-CD40L engagement) required alongside antigen recognition for lymphocyte activation, not to a mutation process affecting binding affinity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tolerance is the state of unresponsiveness to self antigen, unrelated to variable-region point mutations that raise affinity for a foreign epitope.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anergy is a specific form of functional unresponsiveness following incomplete lymphocyte activation, not the process of accumulating affinity-raising mutations.
explanations.D: Correct. Accumulation of point mutations in the immunoglobulin variable regions that increase antibody binding affinity for its specific antigen is precisely what affinity maturation names — the somatic-hypermutation-driven refinement of the antibody response over the course of an immune response. This somatic-hypermutation-driven refinement is what distinguishes a late, high-affinity antibody response from the lower-affinity antibody typically seen earlier in an immune response.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Molecular mimicry describes cross-reactivity between a pathogen antigen and a self antigen (a mechanism implicated in some autoimmune disease), not the process of raising antibody affinity through variable-region mutation.

questions.learning_objective: Name affinity maturation as the term for point mutations increasing antibody-antigen binding affinity.

questions.title: Immunoglobulins tagging antigens for destruction and removal by effector cells — this process is termed:
questions.question: Immunoglobulins can tag antigens for destruction and removal by effector cells. This process is termed

explanations.A: Correct. Opsonization is the process by which immunoglobulin (typically IgG) coats — tags — an antigen or microbe, so that phagocytes and other effector cells bearing the appropriate Fc receptors recognise and remove the tagged particle far more efficiently than they would an untagged one. This antibody-and-complement-mediated tagging is exactly what 'enhancing destruction and removal by effector cells' describes, distinguishing it from mechanisms that act on the microbe's binding ability (neutralization) or kill an antibody-coated host cell (ADCC).
explanations.B: Incorrect. ADCC is antibody-directed killing of an already antibody-coated target CELL by an effector cell (such as an NK cell); it describes a specific killing mechanism against a cell, not the general tagging-for-removal process asked about here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neutralization is antibody blocking a microbe or toxin from binding host cells, not tagging it for removal by effector cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complement activation is a separate antibody-triggered cascade with its own downstream products (one of which, C3b, is itself an opsonin); it is not synonymous with the immunoglobulin-tagging process described.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Agglutination is antibody cross-linking particulate antigen into clumps, not tagging antigen specifically for effector-cell-mediated destruction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify opsonization as immunoglobulin tagging antigen for destruction and removal by effector cells.

questions.title: The constant region of the five major heavy-chain types determines the immunoglobulin molecule's:
questions.question: The constant region of the five major types of heavy chains of immunoglobulin molecules determines the molecule's

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epitope is a property of the antigen being recognised, not of the antibody's own heavy-chain constant region.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Fab fragment is built from the variable region (plus CH1/CL), the antigen-binding portion, not defined by the heavy-chain constant region as a whole.
explanations.C: Correct. An immunoglobulin's isotype (class — IgM, IgG, IgA, IgD or IgE) is determined by the constant region of its heavy chain (mu, gamma, alpha, delta or epsilon respectively); this is exactly why isotype switching changes the constant region while leaving the variable-region-encoded antigen specificity untouched. This is exactly why isotype switching changes the constant region (and therefore isotype) while leaving the variable-region-encoded antigen specificity completely untouched.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A tyrosine-based activation motif (such as ITAM) is a signalling feature of the BCR's associated Ig-alpha/Ig-beta chains, not a property determined by the heavy-chain constant region.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The variable domain determines antigen-binding specificity, not isotype, which is a constant-region property.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the heavy-chain constant region as what determines an immunoglobulin's isotype.

questions.title: In immediate (type I) hypersensitivity to dust mites, cross-linking of which molecule triggers mediator release?
questions.question: In an individual with an immediate hypersensitivity (allergy) to dust mites, cross linking of which of the following dust mite-specific molecules will trigger inflammatory mediator release?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histamine is the released mediator, the downstream product of the reaction — not the molecule that is cross-linked to trigger it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. IgA is not the isotype bound to mast-cell Fc-epsilon receptors and involved in classic immediate hypersensitivity.
explanations.C: Correct. In an individual with immediate (type I) hypersensitivity to dust mites, cross-linking of allergen-specific IgE molecules already bound to mast-cell surface Fc-epsilon receptors, by the allergen itself, triggers mast-cell degranulation and release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine. Once cross-linked, these surface-bound IgE molecules trigger the mast cell's internal signalling cascade that leads to degranulation and mediator release.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgG is not the isotype responsible for classic immediate (type I) hypersensitivity; that role belongs specifically to IgE.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Mast cells are the effector cells that degranulate in response to the cross-linking event; they are not themselves the dust-mite-specific molecule being cross-linked.

questions.learning_objective: Identify allergen-specific IgE as the molecule whose cross-linking on mast cells triggers immediate hypersensitivity mediator release.

questions.title: Regarding antibody-mediated and cell-mediated immunity, which statement is most accurate?
questions.question: Regarding antibody-mediated immunity and cell mediated immunity, which one of the following is the most accurate?

options.A: Antibody-mediated immunity helps to prevent graft rejection
options.B: Antibody-mediated immunity protects against anaphylactic shock
options.C: Antibody-mediated immunity protects against autoimmune diseases
options.D: Cell mediated immunity neutralizes extracellular viruses
options.E: Cell mediated immunity protects against fungal infections

explanations.A: Incorrect. Graft rejection is chiefly a cell-mediated (T-cell-driven) process; antibody-mediated immunity does not help prevent it — indeed, antibody (in hyperacute rejection) can actively drive rejection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anaphylactic shock is itself a harmful antibody-driven (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction, not something antibody-mediated immunity protects against.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Autoimmune disease is often driven, not prevented, by dysregulated antibody and/or cell-mediated responses against self antigen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neutralising extracellular viruses (and toxins) directly in blood or tissue fluid is an antibody-mediated function, not a cell-mediated one.
explanations.E: Correct. Of the effector roles of antibody-mediated versus cell-mediated immunity, cell-mediated immunity (T cells, macrophages, NK cells) is the arm that defends against fungal infections, in contrast to antibody-mediated immunity's chief role against extracellular bacteria, toxins and free virus. This paired antibody-mediated-versus-cell-mediated contrast is exactly the kind of distinction this bank's distractors are built to probe from multiple angles.

questions.learning_objective: Identify fungal infection defence as a cell-mediated, not antibody-mediated, immune function.

questions.title: Which is most likely to induce an IgM response without helper T-cell participation?
questions.question: Which one of the following is most likely to induce an IgM antibody response without the participation of helper T cells?

options.C: Pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide conjugated to diphtheria toxoid

explanations.A: Incorrect. Diphtheria toxoid is a protein antigen and is thymus-dependent, requiring T-cell help rather than bypassing it.
explanations.B: Correct. A pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide left unconjugated is a classic thymus-independent antigen and drives an IgM response without helper-T-cell participation, because its repetitive polysaccharide epitopes cross-link enough BCR molecules to activate the B cell directly. Conjugating that same polysaccharide to a protein carrier is precisely the strategy used to convert it into a thymus-dependent immunogen capable of eliciting memory and isotype switching.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conjugating the same polysaccharide to a protein carrier (diphtheria toxoid) converts it into a thymus-DEPENDENT antigen, precisely the opposite of the T-cell-independent pattern asked about — this conjugate strategy is in fact how polysaccharide vaccines are engineered to generate T-cell help, memory and isotype switching.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tetanus toxoid is a protein antigen and is thymus-dependent, like diphtheria toxoid.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Toxic shock syndrome toxin is a superantigen, which nonspecifically activates T cells via direct MHC-II/TCR cross-linking — a different mechanism from the T-cell-independent B-cell activation asked about here.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an unconjugated polysaccharide antigen as inducing a T-cell-independent IgM response, unlike its conjugated form.

questions.title: Which statement most accurately describes IgA, the first line of mucosal defence?
questions.question: IgA is the first line of defense against infections at the mucous membranes. Which of the following statements most accurately describes IgA?

options.A: Complement fixation tests for IgA will be positive if specific IgA is present
options.B: IgA can be destroyed by bacterial proteases produced by certain bacterial species
options.D: IgA is not found in saliva, therefore an IgA diagnostic test on saliva will be of no value
options.E: IgA is a small molecule with monomeric form only

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgA does not fix complement via the classical pathway the way IgM and IgG do; a complement-fixation-positive result is not a meaningful description of specific IgA presence.
explanations.B: Correct. Secretory IgA can be inactivated by bacterial IgA proteases — enzymes produced by certain mucosal pathogens (such as Neisseria and Haemophilus species) that cleave IgA at its hinge region, undermining mucosal immunity and helping these organisms colonise mucosal surfaces despite a functioning IgA response. This bacterial countermeasure is a genuine clinical vulnerability of mucosal antibody defence, distinct from IgA's presence in colostrum and saliva, both of which are real and diagnostically useful.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgA is present in colostrum, and is in fact the most abundant antibody isotype in colostrum, not absent from it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgA is present in saliva, which is exactly why salivary IgA testing has real diagnostic value; it is not absent there.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Secretory IgA exists chiefly as a dimer (with an attached secretory component and J chain), not exclusively as a monomer.

questions.learning_objective: State that secretory IgA can be inactivated by bacterial IgA proteases produced by certain mucosal pathogens.

questions.title: Which immunoglobulin has no known function, low serum concentration, and functions as a B-cell surface antigen receptor?
questions.question: Which of the following immunoglobulins has no known function, is found in the serum in low concentrations and is present on the surface of B lymphocytes (may function as an antigen receptor)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgA has a well-defined mucosal-defence function and is the dominant antibody at mucous membranes and in secretions, unlike the isotype described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. IgM has clear effector functions — it is the most efficient complement activator and the first isotype secreted in a primary response — and is not the isotype with 'no known function.'
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgE has a well-defined function in parasite defence and mast-cell/basophil binding (mediating immediate hypersensitivity), unlike the isotype described here.
explanations.D: Correct. Among the five immunoglobulin isotypes, IgD is distinctive for having no known independent effector function of its own; it circulates in serum only at low concentration and is instead found, together with IgM, on the surface of naive B lymphocytes, where it functions as part of the B-cell antigen receptor (BCR). This absence of an independent effector role is precisely what distinguishes IgD from every other antibody isotype, each of which does have a defined protective function.
explanations.E: Incorrect. IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin with well-characterised effector functions (opsonization, complement fixation, placental transfer), not a low-concentration isotype of unknown function.

questions.learning_objective: Identify IgD as the isotype with no known effector function, present at low serum concentration and serving as a B-cell antigen receptor.

questions.title: A patient with defective CD40L and recurrent pyogenic infections has elevated IgM due to:
questions.question: A young patient with severe recurrent pyogenic bacterial infection, but with normal T cell and B cell numbers. Lab testing reveals that CD4 T helper cells have a defective CD40L molecule. As a result Humoral Immunity reveals a significant elevation in which of the following immunoglobulins? What is the cause?

options.A: IgA/ due to recurrent mucosal infections
options.B: IgM/ due to defective isotype switching
options.C: IgG/ due to secondary immune response by the recurrent pyogenic infections
options.D: IgD/ due to defective CD4 helper function
options.E: IgE/ due to allergic response to certain proteins of pyogenic bacteria

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgA is not the isotype elevated in CD40L deficiency; the defect blocks isotype switching broadly, leaving IgM elevated rather than raising IgA specifically.
explanations.B: Correct. A patient with recurrent pyogenic infections, normal T- and B-cell numbers, and CD4+ T-helper cells lacking functional CD40 ligand has X-linked Hyper-IgM syndrome: because CD40L-CD40 engagement is the specific molecular trigger for isotype (class-switch) recombination, its absence blocks class switching, so B cells remain unable to switch out of IgM, producing a significant IgM elevation (with low IgG/IgA/IgE) rather than an elevation of another isotype. Because class switching itself is blocked, the humoral response is effectively stuck producing only the unswitched isotype, explaining both the IgM elevation and the accompanying susceptibility to pyogenic infection from low IgG.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgG is characteristically LOW, not elevated, in Hyper-IgM syndrome, since class switching to IgG is exactly what is blocked by the CD40L defect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IgD is not the elevated isotype in this condition, and the underlying cause is defective isotype switching from the CD40L defect, not a broader 'defective CD4 helper function' framing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. IgE is likewise low, not elevated, in Hyper-IgM syndrome, and the cause is the specific CD40L-CD40 signalling defect, not an allergic response.

questions.learning_objective: Identify CD40L deficiency (Hyper-IgM syndrome) as the cause of a humoral immunodeficiency with elevated IgM from defective isotype switching.

questions.title: Which antibody predominates in the secondary response and reaches the highest concentration in the fetus?
questions.question: Which antibody is the predominant antibody in the secondary immune response, and has the greatest concentration of the five immunoglobulins in the fetus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. IgA is not the predominant secondary-response isotype and does not cross the placenta to reach high fetal concentration; it reaches the infant instead via breast milk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. IgM is the predominant PRIMARY-response isotype and does not cross the placenta; any IgM found in a fetus or newborn is produced by the fetus itself, not transferred from the mother.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IgD is present at low serum concentration in general and is not the predominant secondary-response or fetal isotype.
explanations.D: Correct. IgG is both the predominant antibody isotype of the secondary (memory, anamnestic) immune response, reflecting isotype-switched memory B cells, and the immunoglobulin present at the greatest concentration in the fetus, because IgG alone among the isotypes crosses the placenta from the maternal circulation. No other isotype combines both of these properties: IgM dominates the primary response and stays in the mother, IgA and IgD do neither.

questions.learning_objective: Identify IgG as both the predominant secondary-response antibody and the isotype present in the highest concentration in the fetus.

questions.question: Individuals with a genetic deficiency of C6 have:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Terminal complement (C6) deficiency is not classically associated with decreased resistance to viral infections; the classic association is with Neisseria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C6 deficiency is not classically linked to increased hypersensitivity reactions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C6 deficiency is not a recognised cause of increased cancer frequency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C6 deficiency is not the classic complement deficiency linked to autoimmunity (that association is more classically made with early classical-pathway deficiencies such as C1q, C2 or C4).
explanations.E: Correct. This pattern generalises to the other terminal components (C5, C7, C8, C9), all of which share the same Neisseria-susceptibility association when deficient.

questions.learning_objective: Identify terminal complement (C6) deficiency as a cause of increased susceptibility to Neisseria bacteremia.

questions.title: Patients with severely reduced C3 levels tend to have:
questions.question: Patients with severely reduced C3 levels tend to have:

options.A: Increased numbers of severe viral infections
options.B: Increased numbers of severe pyogenic infections
options.C: Loss of delayed hypersensitivity reaction to Tuberculin

explanations.A: Incorrect. C3 deficiency is not classically linked to increased severe viral infections; antiviral defence relies more on cell-mediated and interferon-based mechanisms.
explanations.B: Correct. explanations.D: Incorrect. C3 deficiency is not a recognised cause of increased malignancy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. C3 deficiency is not classically associated with hemolytic anemia; that pattern is more associated with disorders of complement regulation on red cells (such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, a CD59/DAF-deficiency disorder) rather than C3 deficiency itself.

questions.title: Which of the following does NOT describe mannose-binding lectin (MBL)?
questions.question: Which of the following doesn't describe MBL (mannan binding lectin)?

options.A: It is a pattern recognition receptor
options.B: Found on the surface of macrophages
options.C: Binds to the sugar mannose on bacterial cells

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES describe MBL). MBL is a genuine pattern-recognition receptor, recognising a conserved microbial sugar pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this DOES describe MBL). MBL is found on macrophage surfaces (and circulates in serum) as part of its recognition/opsonizing role.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES describe MBL). MBL specifically binds the sugar mannose on bacterial cell surfaces, which is the basis of its name and function.

Its innate, germline-encoded recognition of a conserved bacterial sugar pattern is exactly what distinguishes MBL's mechanism from the antigen-specific receptors of adaptive immunity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mannose-binding lectin as an innate, not adaptive, pattern-recognition molecule.

questions.title: Regarding the complement pathway, which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.question: Regarding the complement pathway, which one of the following is the MOST accurate?

options.A: C3 convertase protects normal cells from lysis by complement
options.B: C3a is a decay acceleration factor and causes the rapid decay of bacteria
options.C: Gram positive bacteria are more likely to be killed by complement than Gram negative
options.D: The membrane attack complex is formed as a result of activation of the classic pathway, but not by activation of the alternative pathway
options.E: The first time a person is exposed to a microorganism, the alternative pathway is more likely to be activated than the classic pathway

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is decay-accelerating factor (DAF), a distinct regulatory protein, that protects normal cells from complement lysis by dissociating convertases — the C3 convertase itself is the enzyme complex that DRIVES the cascade forward, not a protective mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C3a is an anaphylatoxin, not a decay-accelerating factor; DAF is the separate protein that causes convertase decay.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria, with their thick peptidoglycan cell wall, characteristically resist direct complement-mediated (MAC) lysis more than Gram-negative bacteria do, the reverse of this statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Membrane Attack Complex is assembled from C5b onward regardless of which upstream pathway (classical, alternative or lectin) generated the C5 convertase; both the classical and alternative pathways lead to MAC formation.
explanations.E: Correct. Because the classical complement pathway requires an antigen-antibody complex to trigger C1, it cannot fire on a person's first-ever exposure to a microorganism, before any specific antibody has been generated; the alternative pathway, triggered directly by foreign surfaces independent of antibody, is therefore the pathway more likely to be activated on that first exposure, with the classical pathway becoming more prominent only once specific antibody has developed. Once specific antibody has been generated after that first exposure, the classical pathway becomes available and can act alongside the alternative pathway on any subsequent encounter.

questions.title: A 20-year-old with non-tender limb swelling and throat fullness likely has angioedema from:
questions.question: Your patient is a 20-year old woman who complains of swelling on her arms and legs and a feeling of fullness in her throat that makes it difficult to breath. The swellings are not red, hot, or tender. You suspect she may have an angioedema caused by a complement abnormality. Of the following, which one is the most likely explanation?

options.A: She has deficiency in C1 inhibitor
options.B: She has a deficiency in C3b
options.D: She has a deficiency in factor B

explanations.A: Correct. Swelling of the arms, legs and throat that is not red, hot or tender — non-inflammatory angioedema, potentially airway-threatening — is most likely explained by a deficiency of C1 inhibitor (hereditary angioedema): without C1 inhibitor, unchecked classical-pathway and kinin-pathway activation generates excess bradykinin and vasoactive complement fragments, producing this non-inflammatory tissue swelling. Because C1-inhibitor deficiency is a regulatory, not an infection-fighting, defect, these episodes are recurrent and can be triggered by minor trauma or stress rather than by pathogen exposure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A deficiency in C3b would impair opsonization and predispose to recurrent pyogenic infection, not produce this non-inflammatory angioedema pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Excess C9 is not a recognised cause of angioedema; C9 excess is not a described clinical entity in this pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A deficiency in factor B would impair the alternative pathway, again predisposing to infection rather than causing angioedema.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Excess C5a would be expected to cause more inflammatory (not non-inflammatory) effects such as neutrophil recruitment and vascular permeability with typical inflammatory signs, not this classic non-red, non-tender angioedema pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C1-inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema) as the cause of non-inflammatory swelling of the limbs and airway.

questions.title: In complete C3 deficiency, which immune-mediated function would remain intact?
questions.question: A patient is admitted with multiple bacterial infections and is found to have complete absence of C3. Which of the following immune mediated functions would remain intact?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Complement-mediated lysis of bacteria requires the Membrane Attack Complex, downstream of C3; it is lost, not spared, in complete C3 deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opsonization is chiefly mediated by C3b, generated directly from C3; it is abolished by complete C3 deficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Generation of the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a both require C3 cleavage (C5a generation itself requires C5 convertase, built on C3b); this is lost in C3 deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neutrophil chemotaxis via C5a likewise depends on the C3-dependent cascade reaching C5 cleavage, so it is impaired in C3 deficiency.
explanations.E: Correct. C3 is required for lysis, opsonization, anaphylatoxin generation and chemotaxis — so a patient with complete absence of C3 loses all of these — but killing of intracellular bacteria, which depends on cell-mediated mechanisms such as macrophage activation and T-cell-derived interferon-gamma rather than on complement, remains intact despite the C3 deficiency. This spared, complement-independent killing mechanism is a key reason C3-deficient patients, while highly susceptible to extracellular pyogenic infection, are not as broadly immunocompromised as a combined immunodeficiency would predict.

questions.learning_objective: Identify intracellular bacterial killing as the immune function that remains intact in complete C3 deficiency.

questions.title: All of the following activate the alternative complement pathway EXCEPT:
questions.question: All of the following activates the alternative pathway except

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES activate the alternative pathway). Bacterial LPS, the Gram-negative outer-membrane component, is a classic alternative-pathway activator.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this DOES activate the alternative pathway). Some viruses and virus-infected cell surfaces can trigger the alternative pathway directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES activate the alternative pathway). Fungal and yeast cell walls (such as zymosan) are classic alternative-pathway activators.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. Gram-positive bacterial cell walls, whose thick peptidoglycan lacks LPS, are not a classic activator of the alternative pathway in the way LPS, fungal/yeast walls, some viruses and immune complexes are. Recognising which surfaces genuinely trigger the alternative pathway, and which (like Gram-positive peptidoglycan) do not, is exactly the distinction this exception-format question is built to test.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this DOES activate the alternative pathway). IgA-containing immune complexes are a recognised alternative-pathway activator.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the surfaces and molecules that activate the alternative complement pathway, excluding Gram-positive bacterial cell walls.

questions.title: The alternative pathway is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: The alternative pathway of complement is characterized by the functions listed below except:

options.A: Activation of complement components beyond C3 in the cascade
options.D: Generation of chemotactic factors for neutrophils

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES characterise the alternative pathway). It does activate components beyond C3 (C5 through C9), converging on the Membrane Attack Complex.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this DOES characterise the alternative pathway). Properdin stabilises the alternative-pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), a hallmark of this pathway specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES characterise the alternative pathway). Like the classical pathway, it generates the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this DOES characterise the alternative pathway). It generates C5a, a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, like the other pathways.
explanations.E: Correct — this is the exception. The alternative pathway does NOT involve activation of C4, since C4 belongs specifically to the classical and lectin pathways (forming part of the C4b2b convertase), not the alternative pathway, which begins directly from C3. Recognising that the alternative pathway bypasses C1, C4 and C2 entirely, beginning directly at C3, is exactly the distinction this exception-format question tests.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C4 activation as NOT a feature of the alternative complement pathway.

questions.title: DAF (Decay acceleration factor) regulates complement activity by:
questions.question: DAF (Decay acceleration factor) regulates complement activity by:

options.A: Dissociation of C4b2b or C3bBb enzyme complex
options.B: Blocking the binding of C3 convertase to the surface of bacterial cells
options.C: Inhibiting the membrane attack complex from binding to bacterial membranes
options.D: Acting as a cofactor for the cleavage of C3b

explanations.A: Correct. Decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) regulates complement activation specifically by causing dissociation of the C4b2b classical-pathway convertase and the C3bBb alternative-pathway convertase, accelerating their natural decay before they can generate excessive C3b/C5b on a host cell surface. This same convertase-dissociating mechanism is why DAF is essential for protecting normal host cells from being inadvertently destroyed by their own complement system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DAF does not act by blocking convertase binding to bacterial surfaces; it acts on host-cell-surface convertases by dissociating them, and bacterial surfaces generally lack the regulatory proteins that would need this kind of blocking in the first place.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inhibiting MAC binding to bacterial membranes is not DAF's mechanism; DAF acts earlier, at the convertase stage, not at MAC assembly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acting as a cofactor for C3b cleavage is Factor H's (and membrane cofactor protein's) mechanism, not DAF's.
explanations.E: Incorrect. DAF's defining action is dissociating C3 convertases (C4b2b, C3bBb), which indirectly prevents C5 convertase formation, but 'dissociation of C5 convertase' itself is not how DAF's mechanism is classically described.

questions.learning_objective: State DAF's regulatory mechanism as dissociation of the C4b2b and C3bBb convertases.

questions.title: In a C3-deficient individual, antigen-antibody immune complexes will result in:
questions.question: Antigen-antibody immune complexes in a C3-deficient individual will result in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaphylatoxin (C3a/C5a) production requires cleavage of C3 (and C5, downstream of C3); it cannot occur if C3 itself is absent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Factor B is an alternative-pathway component, not activated by a classical-pathway antigen-antibody trigger.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chemotactic-factor (C5a) production requires C5 cleavage, which depends on C3-derived C5 convertase; it does not occur without C3.
explanations.D: Correct. The classical pathway activates its components in the order C1, C4, C2, C3; in a C3-deficient individual, an antigen-antibody immune complex can still activate C1, C4 and C2, since these steps occur upstream of C3 — but the cascade halts at that point. Recognising which specific step of the cascade is blocked, versus which steps remain unaffected, is exactly the distinction this question is built to test.
explanations.E: Incorrect. C5 activation requires the C3-dependent C5 convertase; it cannot proceed if C3 is absent.

questions.learning_objective: State that C2 activation still occurs upstream of a C3 block in a C3-deficient individual.

questions.title: The classical pathway of complement begins with:
questions.question: The classical pathway of complement begins with

options.B: Cleavage and activation of C4, C2 and C3
options.C: IgA binding to a specific epitope

explanations.A: Correct. The classical complement pathway is initiated by an antigen-antibody (immune complex) reaction, which engages and activates C1 (itself composed of C1q, C1r and C1s) — this activation of C1 is the pathway's opening molecular step. Everything that follows — cleavage of C4, then C2, then C3, and eventually assembly of the Membrane Attack Complex — proceeds only after this initiating C1 activation has occurred.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cleavage and activation of C4, C2 and C3 are the sequential STEPS THAT FOLLOW C1 activation, not the beginning of the pathway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is IgG or IgM (not IgA) binding antigen that triggers the classical pathway via C1q engagement; IgA does not activate the classical pathway this way.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Initiation of the Membrane Attack Complex is the pathway's terminal event, not its beginning.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Production of the C3 convertase (C4b2b) is a downstream step, occurring after C1, C4 and C2 activation, not the pathway's first step.

questions.learning_objective: State that the classical complement pathway begins with activation of C1, triggered by an antigen-antibody complex.

questions.title: The classical pathway of complement functions to:
questions.question: The classical pathway of complement functions to

explanations.A: Incorrect. The classical pathway does not cleave immunoglobulin into Fc fragments; that is not a complement function at all.
explanations.B: Correct. The overall function of the classical complement pathway, once triggered by an antigen-antibody complex and carried through C1, C4, C2, C3 and on to the Membrane Attack Complex, is to facilitate destruction of microbes via opsonization, inflammation and direct lysis. Opsonization, generation of inflammatory anaphylatoxins, and direct lysis via the Membrane Attack Complex are the specific mechanisms through which this overall destructive function is carried out.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Recognising specific epitopes on microbes is an antibody-variable-region function, not a function of the complement pathway itself, which is triggered by (not itself performing) that recognition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Triggering B-lymphocyte development is not a function of the classical complement pathway.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Histamine release is a downstream anaphylatoxin (C3a/C5a) effect, a narrower consequence rather than the pathway's overall defining function.

questions.learning_objective: State that the classical complement pathway's overall function is to facilitate destruction of microbes.

questions.title: A boy with recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia, normal immunoglobulins, and low complement levels most likely has:
questions.question: A 3 year old boy had several episodes of pneumonia. Strept pneumoniae was isolated. After treatment with antibiotics the condition resolved but he is evaluated for possible immunodeficiency. Lab reveals normal values for all immunoglobulin isotypes but some levels of complement are depressed. Which of the following deficiencies could explain this problem?

explanations.A: Incorrect. C1 deficiency is rare and, while it can predispose to infection and lupus-like autoimmunity, C3 is the classic, more severe answer for recurrent pyogenic (pneumococcal) infection with normal immunoglobulins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C2 deficiency, the most common inherited complement deficiency, is more classically linked to increased risk of autoimmune disease (SLE-like) and pyogenic infection, but C3 deficiency produces the more severe, classic recurrent-pyogenic-infection pattern this vignette describes.
explanations.C: Correct. C3 sits at the convergence point of all three complement pathways and is essential for opsonization, inflammation and Membrane Attack Complex formation; a child with recurrent bacterial infections despite normal immunoglobulin isotypes should raise suspicion of a complement deficiency, most classically C3, since C3 (not an antibody defect) is what is missing from this clinical picture, and its central role means multiple downstream complement functions/levels appear depressed on testing. Because C3 sits at the convergence point of all three complement pathways, its deficiency can make several downstream complement-dependent readouts appear depressed on a laboratory panel, consistent with the vignette's description.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C4 deficiency, like C2, is more classically associated with SLE-like autoimmunity than with this severe recurrent-pyogenic-infection pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C3 deficiency as the explanation for recurrent pneumococcal infection with normal immunoglobulin isotypes and depressed complement.

questions.title: A man with a 4th episode of disseminated gonorrhea in 5 years most likely has:
questions.question: A man is treated for a fourth episode of disseminated gonorrhea infection in the last 5 years. He had no other predisposing conditions. If he has an immunological defect, which of the following is most likely?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Common variable immunodeficiency presents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections from encapsulated bacteria due to poor antibody production, not this classic recurrent-Neisseria pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. A man treated for a fourth episode of disseminated gonococcal (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) infection in five years, with no other predisposing condition, most likely has a terminal complement pathway defect such as C8 deficiency: because the Membrane Attack Complex is the chief defence against these Gram-negative diplococci, its absence produces this classic recurrent-Neisseria pattern. Because this defect is confined to the complement system, it produces a strikingly narrow, organism-specific susceptibility pattern rather than the broad infection burden seen in antibody or combined immunodeficiencies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia, T-cell deficiency) presents with viral, fungal and opportunistic infections from early life, not this adult recurrent-Neisseria pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Selective IgA deficiency presents with recurrent mucosal/sinopulmonary infections and possible anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products, not this specific recurrent-Neisseria pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Severe combined immunodeficiency presents in infancy with severe, broad susceptibility to virtually all pathogen classes, not an isolated recurrent-Neisseria pattern in an adult with no other predisposing conditions.

questions.learning_objective: Identify C8 (terminal complement) deficiency as the immunological defect underlying recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection.

questions.title: A patient with recurrent abdominal pain and a swollen lip (hereditary angioedema) is expected to show:
questions.question: A patient has been hospitalized three times for periumbilical abdominal pain and is complaining now of swollen lip. What laboratory findings in this patient is expected?

options.A: Abnormal superoxide anion production by neutrophils

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abnormal neutrophil superoxide production is the defect in chronic granulomatous disease, an unrelated phagocyte disorder, not hereditary angioedema.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hereditary angioedema is a complement/kinin regulatory disorder, not a T-cell functional defect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T-cell numbers are normal in hereditary angioedema, which is not a T-cell immunodeficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Defective neutrophil chemotaxis is not the expected finding; it points to a different, phagocyte-chemotaxis disorder, not C1-inhibitor deficiency.
explanations.E: Correct. A patient hospitalised repeatedly for abdominal pain and swollen lips, consistent with hereditary angioedema from C1-inhibitor deficiency, is expected on laboratory testing to have reduced C4 levels: unchecked classical-pathway activation, unrestrained by C1 inhibitor, continuously consumes C4 (and C2), so C4 characteristically runs low even between attacks. This laboratory pattern, together with the recurrent non-inflammatory swelling episodes, is what distinguishes hereditary angioedema from an allergic (histamine-mediated) cause of swelling, which would not show this complement consumption pattern.

questions.learning_objective: State that reduced C4 levels are the expected laboratory finding in hereditary angioedema from C1-inhibitor deficiency.

questions.title: Patients with C5 through C9 complement deficiencies are most susceptible to which infections?
questions.question: Patients with C5 through C9 complement deficiencies are most likely to be susceptible to which of the following infections?

explanations.A: Incorrect. AIDS is caused by HIV infection and CD4 T-cell loss, unrelated to terminal complement deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giardiasis is classically associated with IgA deficiency or splenic dysfunction, not terminal complement deficiency.
explanations.C: Correct. Deficiencies of any of the terminal complement components, C5 through C9, which together assemble the Membrane Attack Complex, are most classically associated with susceptibility to Neisseria infections (meningococcal and gonococcal), because MAC-mediated lysis is this Gram-negative diplococcus genus's chief vulnerability to complement. This same MAC-dependent vulnerability explains why C5, C6, C7, C8 and C9 deficiencies all share this same classic Neisseria-susceptibility association.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Histoplasmosis is associated with cell-mediated immunodeficiency (impaired T-cell/macrophage function), not terminal complement deficiency.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pneumococcal infections are classically linked to antibody/opsonization defects (such as early complement component C3 deficiency, asplenia or antibody deficiency), not specifically to terminal (C5-C9) complement deficiency.

questions.learning_objective: State that C5-C9 (terminal complement) deficiency is classically associated with susceptibility to Neisseria infections.

questions.title: Which statement best describes complement's protective role against foreign microorganisms?
questions.question: Complement is a series of important host proteins that provides protection against invasion by foreign microorganisms. Which of the following statements best describe complement:

options.B: Complement is activated by IgE antibody classes
options.C: Complement plays a minor role in the inflammatory response
options.D: Microorganisms agglutinate in the presence of complement but do not lyse
options.E: Complement protects the host from pneumococcal infection through C1, C2 and C4

explanations.A: Incorrect. Complement enhances, rather than inhibits, phagocytosis, chiefly through the opsonin C3b.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The classical pathway is activated by IgG and IgM, not IgE, engaging C1q.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Complement plays a major, not minor, role in acute inflammation, via the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a among other effects.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complement-coated microorganisms are typically opsonized for enhanced phagocytosis (and, for susceptible organisms, can be directly lysed by the MAC), not merely agglutinated without further consequence.
explanations.E: Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram-positive organism with a thick peptidoglycan cell wall, resists direct lysis by the Membrane Attack Complex, so the host is protected from pneumococcal infection chiefly by the classical pathway (C1, C2 and C4, activated by anti-capsular antibody) generating the opsonin C3b, which promotes phagocytic clearance rather than lysis. This explains why vaccination strategies against pneumococcus target generating anti-capsular antibody to drive this opsonizing classical-pathway route, rather than relying on direct complement-mediated lysis of the organism.

questions.learning_objective: State that complement protects against pneumococcal infection chiefly through classical-pathway (C1, C2, C4) opsonization, since Gram-positive organisms resist complement-mediated lysis.
